title: Nachmanides' other way
hook: a more mystical approach to the same texts

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: controversy, then canon. Accused, critiqued, banned, and then studied at the center. Did you give someone credit before you disagreed? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

A hot afternoon. Abraham sits at the opening of his tent, looks up, and sees three men standing nearby. He runs to meet them, bows, and hurries Sarah to bake bread while he picks out a calf. A homely scene from Genesis. Now hand that same scene to two great rabbis named Moses. One says it all happened in a prophetic vision. The other says those words contradict Scripture. Same text, same tent, two very different readings. Today's word is the second reader, and his other way.
screen: `THREE MEN AT THE TENT.` → `A VISION?` → `OR SOMETHING ELSE?`

segments.voice: Nachmanides' other way. His name was Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, known as the Ramban, a rabbi from Girona, in Catalonia. Turn his way four ways. First, he argues out loud. In the Guide, Maimonides reads the visit of the three men as something Abraham saw in a prophetic vision. In his commentary on Genesis, the Ramban quotes him, then pushes back hard: these words, he says, contradict Scripture, and one shouldn't listen to them. If it was only a vision, why the bread, the calf, the hurrying? He reads the visitors as real messengers, seen in a form people could see. Second, the offerings. Maimonides explains the sacrifices as a gentle step: people in the ancient world knew worship by offerings, so the Torah kept the form and turned it toward God alone. The Ramban objects. The Torah calls an offering "of a sweet savour unto the LORD." He sees in it a picture for the one who brings it: what is done to the animal should make the person think, this should have been me, and the offering stands in their place. Third, the way of truth. Here and there in his commentary, the Ramban drops a short hint and says the meaning is known by the way of truth. That phrase points to a hidden, mystical layer of the Torah, the tradition known as Kabbalah. He hints. He doesn't spell it out. Fourth, two ways, one Torah. Maimonides reaches for reason and philosophy. The Ramban reaches for the plain story and for hidden depths. Both read the same verses with great seriousness. Neither erased the other. Students still open both, side by side, and learn from the argument.
screen: `HE ARGUES OUT LOUD.` · `A SWEET SAVOUR UNTO THE LORD.` · `THE WAY OF TRUTH.` · `TWO WAYS, ONE TORAH.` · then, large: `TWO WAYS OF THINKING.`

segments.voice: Find a comfortable way to sit, and breathe. Pick one question that matters to you. Why do people suffer. What happens after death. Why pray. Now give it two readers. One answers with careful reasons, step by step. The other answers with a story, or a sense that something deeper is hidden there. Let each speak for a few breaths without interrupting. You don't have to choose a winner. Just notice what each one sees that the other misses. The bell holds the time.
Nachmanides' other way. The Ramban's reading of the Torah: close to the plain story, open to a hidden way of truth, and willing to argue with Maimonides by name. Today's word.
Your line: two ways of thinking. Today, when a question comes up, ask how a second, very different reader would answer it. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles, and students often read it alongside other commentators, comparing how each one reads the same verse.

fork.setup: you're the Ramban, and Maimonides has written that Abraham's three visitors came in a prophetic vision. what do you do?
options: accept it quietly out of respect.
quote him and argue that it contradicts Scripture.
leave the chapter out of your commentary.
fork.reveal: he quotes the Guide and pushes back hard. yet both men's books are still read side by side.

original.note: Hebrew: the way of truth, the Ramban's phrase for a hidden, mystical meaning of a verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: rabbis agree on what the Torah means.
what it means: the Ramban read the same verses as Maimonides and argued with him, toward the plain story and a hidden depth.
what a scholar hears: Ramban on Genesis 18:1 against Guide 2:42, and on Leviticus 1:9 against Guide 3:32 and 3:46, with his allusions 'al derekh ha-emet.

notes: Ramban on Genesis 18:1 paraphrased: he cites Guide 2:42 and says such words contradict Scripture and it is forbidden to listen to them (stronger: 'all the more so to believe them'). Softened to 'one shouldn't listen to them'. Please confirm.
Ramban's reading of the visitors ('real messengers, seen in a form people could see') is a simplification of his discussion of angels appearing in human form and of 'clothed' sight; please check.

Ramban on Leviticus 1:9 paraphrased: the one bringing the offering should feel that what is done to the animal ought to have been done to him, and the offering is a substitute; and his objection to Guide 3:32. Please confirm.
Leviticus 1:9 JPS 1917: confirm 'of a sweet savour unto the LORD' (JPS 1917 'an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD').
'the tradition that would come to be called Kabbalah' and the characterization of 'al derekh ha-emet as kabbalistic allusion: please confirm phrasing for this path; day 1171 introduces Kabbalah.
'Students still open both, side by side' kept general; howItsDone says the Ramban is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles (Mikraot Gedolot). Please confirm.

Editor: Maimonides' view of sacrifices restated accurately (a concession that redirects a familiar form of worship to God, not 'a step away' from it); Ramban's substitution reading made clearer; dropped the dating claim 'would come to be called Kabbalah'; added Guide 3:46, which the Ramban's Leviticus 1:9 comment answers; practice opener varied.
